    Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
    • Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it noted was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
    • Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

    Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it noted was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.

    Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.

    The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.

    The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.

    With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.

    Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted.

    Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, noted rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

    He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

    Industry observers note that BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

    According to recent reports, oleksiy stated rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.

    BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

    A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

    While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.

    According to recent reports, local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities noted an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.

    Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in Ukraine.

    Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.

    Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

    In a recent development, the same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.

    Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

    Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

    Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, stated a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.

    His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who noted the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.

    The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kit.

    Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.

    International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

    Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

    Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University mentioned "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.

    Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’.
    • The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
    • Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was revealed as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’.

    The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

    Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was revealed as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

    Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara noted the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

    Industry observers note that the Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”.

    She remarked: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

    “Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama stated. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”.

    Recent findings suggest that kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

    Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

    Associated Press contributed to this report.

    Tech Report: Instagram’s fresh tool for creators targets unauthorized reposts and AI-modified videos

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company declared Tuesday.
    • The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos.
    • Instagram claims the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company declared Tuesday. The feature, called “content protection,” is already available on Facebook and is designed to detect when creators’ original videos are being used without their permission. The company is also expanding the tool to address AI content, not just conventional reposting.

    The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos.

    Instagram claims the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos. When Instagram detects a match for one of a creator’s Reels uploaded by another user, it sends the creator an alert. Creators can then choose to block the video from being viewed on both Instagram and Facebook to hide the matched content. They can also choose to add an “original by” label on the content that links viewers of the matching video back to their original video.

    Additionally, creators can choose to keep the match visible while monitoring its performance or release their claim on the reel, allowing it to remain visible on Meta’s platforms.

    Industry observers note that the tool will also begin detecting AI-generated videos that reuse audio from creators’ original content, even when the visuals have been altered. This upgrade will initially be tested with a small group of creators in the coming weeks. The organization intends to expand access to this feature to creators who enroll in content protection on both Instagram and Facebook soon.

    Instagram indicates it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repost others’ work.

    Creators who are eligible for content protection will see a notification in their activity feed. Once they enroll, every original video they post to Instagram going forward is automatically protected. They can also choose to retroactively protect eligible videos they’ve already posted by manually selecting them.

    If creators have permitted certain profiles to use their work, such as their second profile or a brand, they can add them to their allow list so their videos won’t be flagged as matches.

    Tuesday’s announcement marks another step in Instagram’s ongoing efforts to give creators greater control over their content and protect the originality of their work.

Unlike recent communications outages, this is a planned interruption that FEMA is required to run every three years.     You’ll hear high-pitched alert tones and the following test message:.

FEMA runs tests like this when there’s not an actual emergency so it can find technical and operational concerns with the Emergency Alert System. If there is a real emergency or severe weather event today, the test will run on December 3rd instead.

    Recent findings suggest that president Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday to begin a 48-hour Asia trip in which he will meet with Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.

    Mr. Trump was scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours in Manila, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where he was expected to meet with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

    The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.

    In a recent development, mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

    Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, after issuing tariffs on countries across the region, even allies. Those moves added to a sentiment in Asia that the United States was not a reliable partner but rather one that treasured its commercial interests over its security interests. The only event of substance on the president’s schedule on Tuesday — signing what he had called a “trade deal” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.

    Sources indicate that mr. Trump met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.

    In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

    Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.

    According to recent reports, mr. Trump also stated, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.

    Here’s what else we’re covering:.

    Protests: Thousands of demonstrators assembled in downtown Manila on Tuesday in opposition to Mr. Trump’s visit and to a U.S.-led initiative called Pax Silica, which aims to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. Read more ›.

    Recent findings suggest that asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, mentioned on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim prepares to attend the summit.

    Sources indicate that mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.

    Industry observers note that as the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.

    A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.

    On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.

    According to recent reports, before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin remarked that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a latest chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”.

    Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.

    During the final meeting of the day, with ASEAN leaders, President Trump told President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines:  “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great. I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”.

    It has been revealed that the only event of substance on President Trump’s schedule today, the signing of a trade deal between the United States and Thailand, did not happen because it was still being finalized. Trump told reporters that “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. imports” and that the United States would provide tariff relief, but the two sides signed only a memorandum about the agreement. The president said the deal would be done in the coming weeks.

    During an address to Quad leaders, President Trump called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, which is a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Modi as he stood with other leaders and took a few questions, calling him a “very tough man.”.

    In a recent development, india and the United States are navigating a rocky patch in their relationship, largely tied to trade and India’s purchases of Russian oil.     The Nvidia turmoil and its implications for the U.S.-China relationship is a backdrop to President Trump’s visit. In Hong Kong trading, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent, and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent.

    President Trump is expected to meet with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul of Thailand on Tuesday in Manila to sign what the White House has described as a “trade deal.”.

    But Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs remarked in a statement on Tuesday that Bangkok was expecting to agree only on a “joint statement marking progress in negotiations.”.

    Mr. Trump later reduced the tariffs to 19 percent, before the U.S. Supreme Court struck them down in February. The administration eventually found a way to still impose 12.5 percent tariffs on Thai goods.

    Pavida Pananond, an economist at Thammasat Business School in Bangkok, stated, “The level of trust Thailand has in the U.S. is not at the same level as before all this economic weaponization of tariffs.”.

    According to recent reports, after handing over the chairmanship of ASEAN to Singapore, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines held a news conference. “President Trump has just arrived,” he noted. “He is waiting for us to go to him and to invite him to this really very informal kind of summit.”.

    Mr. Marcos ended his comments by apologizing for not taking more questions from journalists. “I cannot keep the president of the United States waiting,” he remarked. “Sorry.”.

    Industry observers note that at his hotel, President Trump sat down for a meeting with Quad leaders and took a few questions.     Several hundred activists massed on Tuesday in central Manila to march to the Philippine International Convention Center, the venue for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

    By the time President Trump landed in the city, the ranks of the protesters had swelled to thousands.

    Most of the demonstrators were university students who stated that they were fed up with the government, which they said was more focused on preserving its relationship with the United States than helping impoverished Filipinos.

    Cinna Sison, 18, who studies European languages at the University of the Philippines, stated they were inspired by the recent mass protests in France.

    According to recent reports, “I love the French,” she mentioned. “They know how to protest.”.

    In a recent development, ms. Sison stated she had worn colorful makeup to mark her first time attending a demonstration. “I am here to show my solidarity with fellow young activists. We are here to show our disgust to the fascist Trump and to Marcos for kowtowing to his every wish,” she said, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines.

    Mr. Trump is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before he heads to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

    It has been revealed that the Philippine president, who earlier this year described Washington as a “steadfast partner,” has stated little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump. His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.

    Industry observers note that in Manila, Ms. Sison wore a red scarf on her head and a red shirt with the words “Silicone not Silica” — a reference to Pax Silica, a U.S.-led consortium of countries aiming to create artificial intelligence supply chains independent of China.

    According to recent reports, ms. Sison added that Pax Silica was a symbolic return of the Americans to the Philippines, the site of former U.S. military bases, as Washington leaned on a regional ally to counter China.

    According to recent reports, “Neighborliness is crucial, but it is not important to be subservient to U.S. interests,” she said.

    “We want to show how Trump is a warmonger, while Marcos is a lap dog,” she remarked. “They are very disrespectful to Filipinos. Trump was welcomed in a grand way and yet we Filipinos are maltreated.”.

    President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday, beginning a trip to Asia in which he will attend an ASEAN summit, greet members of the Quad, then travel to China for an APEC meeting.

    Here’s what those acronyms mean, as well as some highlights from previous summits — including gold crowns and awkward handshakes.

    The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum is a group of 21 member economies, most of which are from that region. Its members also include Canada, Mexico, Australia, Russia and the United States. It promotes trade in Asia, but is not a free trade bloc. Its leaders meet annually, with the location rotating each year.

    It has been revealed that meetings between world leaders on the sidelines of the summit can often overshadow the main proceedings. This year, in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, Mr. Trump is expected to meet with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, as well as with Mr. Xi separately.

    Sources indicate that last year, when Mr. Trump visited the South Korean city of Gyeongju during the week of the APEC meeting, President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea gave him a replica of a gold crown that researchers believe was worn by an ancient Korean ruler. Mr. Trump also met with Mr. Xi in the nearby city of Busan, where the two struck a truce in their countries’ trade war.

    A notable incident happened in Sydney, Australia, in 2007, when a group of local television comedians brought an Osama bin Laden look-alike through security. The team came within yards of a hotel where President George W. Bush was staying.

    According to recent reports, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is a grouping of 11 countries — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, East Timor and Vietnam — which promotes political cooperation and stability across the region. Its leaders meet twice annually.

    Recent findings suggest that the bloc was formed in 1967 and represents nearly 700 million people. Its economy and its role in global markets have strengthened in recent years. The United States also sees ASEAN as a geostrategic bulwark against China.

    Industry observers note that in 2009, an ASEAN meeting in Thailand fell into acrimony when Secretary of State Hillary Clinton compared North Korea’s leaders to “small children” when discussing their nuclear program. The country’s leadership, in turn, described Ms. Clinton as a “schoolgirl” and a “pensioner.”.

    In a recent development, during the 2017 ASEAN summit in Manila, Mr. Trump grimaced while jostling with Southeast Asian leaders for an awkward cross-armed handshake that was captured in a group photograph.

    The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue is an informal partnership between Australia, India, Japan and the United States, which was formed in part to counter China. It was proposed by Prime Minister Shinzo Abe of Japan in 2007.

    Beijing opposed the initial discussion, lodging formal diplomatic protests. Australia withdrew in 2008 and the dialogue was put on hold for some time. But the grouping was revived in 2017 on the sidelines of an ASEAN conference.

    Sources indicate that president Biden was the first U.S. president to convene a meeting among the leaders of the nations as a foursome. In 2024, he hosted the Quad leaders at his home in Wilmington, Del. Mr. Trump has appeared to be less enthusiastic about the partnership. Last year, he did not attend the Quad summit in India.

    Sui-Lee Wee and Aie Balagtas See.

    Reporting from the village of Manabayucan in the Philippines and the capital, Manila.

    In May, Roseller Rodriguez, a mayor in the Philippines, was startled to learn from news reports that U.S. officials had arrived in his district to start an artificial intelligence hub.

    He saw a video of senior American and Filipino officials standing on a makeshift stage, unveiling a fresh initiative called Pax Silica.

    Mr. Rodriguez had not been invited. Nor had he ever heard about the hub. Was it a data center? Where would the water and electricity come from? What would happen to the farmers living there?

    Months later, he claims he has few answers.

    Recent findings suggest that “I’m not concerned with the geopolitics of Pax Silica,” Mr. Rodriguez noted in his office in the municipality of Capas. “My problem is Pax Silica will be built in our community.”.

    The United States started Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. The initiative is part of President Trump’s effort to counter Beijing’s economic and technological influence.

    Trump administration officials have cast it as a 21st-century successor to Pax Americana, the era of relative peace among major powers after World War II.

    The significance of Pax Silica, which 26 signatories have joined, has become heightened after revelations that Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, was targeted by Chinese intelligence, exposing the growing geopolitical stakes of the global A.I. race.

    In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce.

    Dozens of Filipino performers greeted President Trump as he descended the stairs of Air Force One onto the tarmac of Ninoy Aquino Airport in Manila, waving flags and playing “Y.M.C.A.” by the Village People on drums and trumpets.

    President Vladimir V. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit this week, Russian state news agencies reported, citing Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesman. Before his departure for China, Putin met on Monday with a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. It was not yet clear whether the North Korean leader would attend the summit.

    President Trump has landed in Manila, lingering on the tarmac for a welcome ceremony before walking alone to Marine One. He has several events tonight, but he will not leave his hotel for them. A meeting with quad leaders, a U.S.-Thailand trade deal signing and a dinner will all be held at the resort where the president is staying. In other words, he showed up late to this summit, and the summit will be coming to him.

    Industry observers note that thousands of protesters have assembled in downtown Manila, chanting in Tagalog, “Trump leave the Philippines.” They are opposed to his Pax Silica A.I. supply chain initiative.

    President Trump’s stopover at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is part of a state visit to the Philippines, where he will be received with a 21-gun salute.

    Recent findings suggest that the last time he met President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, was full of praise for the Filipino leader.

    According to recent reports, “Great family, great family legacy and highly respected in his country,” Mr. Trump said while hosting Mr. Marcos at the White House last year.

    Sources indicate that but that legacy was long considered an obstacle to Mr. Marcos’s political ambitions. He is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986 by a nonviolent uprising. The elder Marcos died in exile in Hawaii, without facing trial on U.S. criminal charges that he had plundered the Philippine Treasury. Years later, a court found his estate liable for torture, summary executions and disappearances.

    The younger Marcos spent years rehabilitating his family’s image and won election in 2022. He is hosting Mr. Trump at his official residence, Malacañang Palace, which was also his childhood home.

    Mr. Marcos and his wife, Liza Marcos, will receive Mr. Trump on Wednesday with a 21-gun salute. Mr. Trump is expected to sign the palace guest book, hold closed-door meetings, pose for a handshake, then attend a state luncheon held in his honor.

    Industry observers note that it is not clear whether Mr. Trump, who has a well-known affinity for autocratic leaders, will meet with Mr. Marcos’s mother, Imelda, 97, with whom he has socialized in Latest York. Ms. Marcos wielded immense power when her husband was president and later came to be known for her flamboyant lifestyle, shoe collection and unexplained wealth.

    According to recent reports, mr. Marcos has noted that when he called to congratulate Mr. Trump on his election victory in November 2024, Mr. Trump asked about Imelda Marcos.

    It has been revealed that “My mother is really his friend, he knows my mother very well,” Mr. Marcos stated, relaying the conversation. “He was asking about her, ‘How’s Imelda?’ I told him she sends her congratulations.”.

    After the pomp and circumstance at Malacañang, which traces its roots to the Spanish colonial era in the Philippines, Mr. Trump is headed to Shenzhen, China. The highlight of that leg of his trip will be a trilateral meeting with two strongmen: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

    Verena Hölzl and Jason Gutierrez.

    For the second year in a row, President Trump is attending the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders, a show of alliance to a region that the United States sees as a strategic and maritime counterweight to China.

    In a recent development, but Mr. Trump reached the gathering, held this year in Manila, only on Tuesday, just as the summit was wrapping up, and he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.

    Sources indicate that mixed signals like this — to say nothing of Mr. Trump’s punishing tariffs — are adding to a widespread belief within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. That leaves the bloc balancing between Washington and Beijing, with which many of its members have deep trade partnerships.

    “They’ve learned that the United States is not reliable, so a lot of the hedging has been away from the United States,” stated Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.

    The Philippines, America’s oldest security ally in Asia, provides a window into this balancing act.

    Sources indicate that after taking office three years ago, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reversed his predecessor’s tilt toward China and pivoted back toward the United States. That stance contributed to many tense encounters between Filipino and Chinese vessels in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing territorial claims.

    Recent findings suggest that as U.S. patrols in the South China Sea have dropped, Mr. Marcos has appeared to be more conciliatory toward Beijing. In August, he remarked that there was a “distinct possibility” that the Philippines and China could partner on oil and gas exploration in those waters despite their territorial feud.

    “Marcos Jr. already has begun a shift toward China, one that a single visit by Trump is unlikely to stop,” Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote last week.

    On Sunday, China and ASEAN failed to agree on a code of conduct in the South China Sea — something the Philippines, which has some of the biggest stakes in the dispute, had vowed to secure while chairing the bloc this year.

    Chester Cabalza, president of International Development and Security Cooperation, a Philippine think tank, said, “Strategically, Manila opens its doors for conciliation with Beijing to stabilize normal ties. But on the ground, the real battle has yet to subside.”.

    According to recent reports, domestically, Mr. Marcos has to walk a tightrope, too.

    Recent findings suggest that “For Filipino fishermen and coastal communities, the South China Sea is not simply about a geopolitical dispute. It concerns livelihoods, access to maritime resources and national dignity,” mentioned Arnaud Leveau, president of the Asia Centre, a Paris-based think tank. Any diplomatic accommodation perceived as sacrificing Filipino interests, he said, would therefore be politically risky.

    According to recent reports, the wider region has been battered by the consequences of another Trump policy: the war in Iran. Southeast Asia depends heavily on oil and gas imports from the Middle East and was roiled by soaring prices of fuel. In the Philippines, crops rotted in fields because farmers could not afford to transport them to markets. In Thailand, public servants were asked to use stairs instead of elevators to reduce energy expenses.

    ASEAN comprises 11 nations — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, and, since last year, East Timor — with vastly different degrees of freedom and wealth. The bloc represents almost 700 million people, or almost 10 percent of the global population.

    Making decisions on a consensus-basis and pledging not to interfere in one other’s internal affairs, the bloc has often been criticized as slow and ineffective, with the situation in Myanmar often cited as an example. A coup in that country in 2021 unleashed a civil war that ranks among the world’s most violent conflicts.

    Myanmar’s leaders remain barred from ASEAN summits, under an agreement that was extended on Monday. Still, almost half of the bloc’s member states have had bilateral engagements with Myanmar since the coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, used stage-managed elections to take the post of president this year. Washington has also recently re-engaged in direct talks with Myanmar.

    Mr. Trump’s attendance at the summit, which concludes with an ASEAN-U.S. meeting, is part of a state visit to the Philippines. He is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before heading to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Mr. Marcos has noted little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump; but earlier this year, he described Washington as a “steadfast partner.” His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.

    Industry observers note that in recent days, hundreds of demonstrators have gathered in Manila to protest Mr. Trump’s visit. They oppose his “Pax Silica” initiative, a move to build a supply chain for the artificial intelligence industry that bypasses China, saying it would exploit Philippine natural resources.

    Renato Reyes, who led one of the protest groups on Sunday afternoon, said, “Marcos is so desperate to welcome Donald Trump that he will roll out the red carpet, even if Trump arrives late for the summit.”.

    Aie Balagtas See contributed reporting from Manila and Damien Cave from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

    In a recent development, president Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

    It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

    Sources indicate that mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence.

    Sources indicate that for Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports.

    The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China.

    The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe.

    Recent findings suggest that the White House has said that Mr. Trump wants to discuss the threat of nuclear proliferation. U.S. officials have expressed concerns about China’s accelerating nuclear buildup, expected to reach 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030.

    In a recent development, the last nuclear arms control treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February. Trump administration officials have said that any latest agreement on nuclear arms control must include China, but Beijing has shown no interest in the topic. China has an estimated 620 nuclear warheads, compared with the more than 5,000 that Russia and the United States have each, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

    U.S. administration officials remarked they did not expect a deal out of the meeting, which they characterized as a starting point for discussions.

    The gathering has prompted concern in Ukraine that Mr. Putin might push for a deal, deciding Ukraine’s fate without Kyiv’s involvement. A U.S. administration official remarked Ukraine was not expected to be part of the discussion between the three leaders.

    Industry observers note that mr. Trump will start his trip in the Philippines, the oldest American treaty ally in the Asia-Pacific region, as the United States faces questions about its support for its partners in a region where China’s military and economic might continues to grow.

    Industry observers note that in Manila, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. plans to discuss with Mr. Trump the South China Sea, where the Philippines and China have competing claims. Philippine officials have noted that they hope Mr. Trump’s visit might result in more American military assistance.

    Mr. Trump is also expected to meet with leaders of ASEAN, a Southeast Asian grouping of 11 nations, as well as a gathering of the so-called Quad grouping of the United States, India, Australia and Japan.

    Industry observers note that prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia said on Sunday that he expected “lots of engagement” with Mr. Trump during the meetings.

    “Obviously, that’s our most vital ally,” he remarked. “But we want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts that are around the world.”.

    Industry observers note that chinese analysts described the meeting of the Quad group, formed in part to counter China, as an effort by Mr. Trump to project power after his party’s defeat in the midterms. “Its symbolic value outweighs its practical value,” Xu Liping, a senior scholar at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, told Shanghai Observer, a state-run outlet.

    According to recent reports, after Manila, Mr. Trump will travel to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, where he will meet Mr. Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.

    Jensen Huang, a key adviser who accompanied Mr. Trump on his last trip to China, will not be by his side. Mr. Huang helped shape the president’s views about technological competition with China and persuaded him to loosen restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.

    Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was collecting intelligence on Mr. Huang for Beijing. China has rejected the allegations, calling them “smears.” Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

    Industry observers note that so far, the president has not raised the concern with Mr. Xi and is not expected to during their meeting on Thursday. But the saga is likely to cause unease in China about whether Washington will impose tighter controls on the export of technology to the country.

    As a result, U.S.-based analysts speculated that Mr. Xi might try to use his personal relationship with Mr. Trump to forestall such restrictions.

    Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, remarked Mr. Huang’s downfall would likely mean “there is going to be more anxiety on the Chinese side about their access to American chips.” She expects Mr. Xi to emphasize the importance of easing U.S. controls on chip exports to China during their meeting.

    Cooperation between China and the United States on artificial intelligence may be more difficult after the Nvidia scandal.

    Still, there may be progress on the creation of a notification system that would allow the countries to alert each other about national security issues related to artificial intelligence, which the two sides agreed to in September.

    “There’s some shared concern on both sides that U.S. or Chinese models might be misused by bad actors and cause damage to the U.S., China, or other countries,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution focusing on China’s technology development.

    Recent findings suggest that when Mr. Xi sits down with Mr. Trump in Shenzhen, he will be dealing with a president who will soon face a newly introduced constraint at home: a Democrat-controlled Congress.

    In a recent development, lawmakers may pressure Mr. Trump to tighten export controls against China or accelerate weapons sales to Taiwan, according to Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser focusing on U.S.-China relations at the International Crisis Group. That means that “Xi will have to work much harder to keep Trump on side,” Mr. Wyne said.

    Mr. Trump will be the first American president to visit China twice in one calendar year.

    Analysts say the leaders’ summits, which have included state visits in Beijing and then in Washington, have been the only thing holding together a fragile détente between the two countries as they clash over A.I., export controls, Taiwan and other concerns.

    Sources indicate that the two sides declared a trade truce last year when they met in Busan, South Korea. That deal, which was to expire this month, has been extended until January.

    China’s restrictions on the export of crucial rare-earth metals and rare-earth magnets, which are needed to manufacture most modern technology, remain one of the most difficult unresolved complications.

    Mr. Trump is likely to raise this with Mr. Xi, according to a senior U.S. administration official who noted that China’s continued restrictions is one reason Washington only agreed to a two-month extension of the trade truce.

    Ana Swanson contributed reporting from Washington, Aie Balagtas See from Manila, and Laura Chung from Sydney, Australia.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Planning a trip is a favorite demo for personal AI assistants: you can try it with Muse, or with Gemini or half a dozen other choices. But while most pitches use travel-planning as part of a general-purpose agent pitch, a latest startup from a Google Maps alum is betting that a specialized travel-planning agent can beat the competition.

    Industry observers note that the company is called Voyage Labs, and on Tuesday it confirmed $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins, with participation from SignalFire and SV Angel. The company looks to use the funding to expand supplier partnerships and grow its engineering team.

    Voyage Labs’ flagship product is called Atlas, meant to work as a personal assistant for your trip-planning, available today in private beta.

    “People can use it to plan their and plan and book and manage their entire journey from the time they have an inspiration to the time they come back home,” indicates co-founder and CEO Manik Gupta.

    Atlas is designed to serve as an always-on assistant throughout the planning process, fielding ideas and doing research on every idea that’s raised. The long time horizon means Atlas can tailor recommendations based on weeks of conversation, while also monitoring real-time price fluctuations and ultimately booking flights and hotels.

    Recent findings suggest that for the Voyage founders, it’s an ideal match between technology and use-case. “trip planning is a project that has its own lifecycle,” states Yogesh Jain, co-founder and CTO of the company. “You’re planning across days and weeks — so long-running agents as a technology matches that very well.”.

    Recent findings suggest that travel assistants are already a crowded field, but Voyage will be starting with a lot of experience in the space. Gupta was previously the Director of Product Management for Google Maps, followed by four years as Chief Product Officer at Uber. As he puts it, “I spent eight years where my only job was to wake up in the morning and go build the map. I’m just very obsessed with that problem.”.

    The biggest question is how Atlas will compete with the multi-purpose AI assistants built by frontier labs. But as Gupta notes, the space is still changing fast, and it’s hard for anyone to be sure what form factors will thrive in the coming years. Ultimately, Voyage is betting that travel is specialized enough to need a specialized product.

    “We are making a bet that this vertical around travel and outdoors is a large enough vertical that it needs a focused product solution,” Manek told TechCrunch. “Ultimately, we believe we can actually stitch together an end-to-end experience that will help owners.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human.
    • The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
    • It has been revealed that the 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human.

    The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

    It has been revealed that the 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

    In a recent development, the growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.

    During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

    Recent findings suggest that after the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”.

    It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”.

    On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

    Recent findings suggest that “We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”.

    The City of Cape Town mentioned in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

    It noted: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”.

    Sources indicate that prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, mentioned the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”.

    The Kremlin remarked it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.

    The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.

    Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

    While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

    Sources indicate that the timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

    The damage after the overnight attack, involving missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.

    Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

    Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

    He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".

    The Ukrainian president also remarked the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images revealed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

    Ukraine's state security service SBU remarked operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it highlighted "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".

    Meanwhile, Ukraine's military remarked the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.

    Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stated the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.

    Recent findings suggest that russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

    For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

    Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

    There was heavy traffic in Kyiv on Tuesday after two major crossings were closed after strikes.

    Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko noted the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - were closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.

    Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.

    Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials remarked, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

    Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

    Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.

    Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

    The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

    The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.

    However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

    This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

    There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

    Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

    In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.

    This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

    Russia's rolled out its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

    Trmnl’s latest digital dashboard features a large color E Ink screen to display photos and artwork.﻿.

    Trmnl’s latest digital dashboard features a large color E Ink screen to display photos and artwork.﻿.

    According to recent reports, trmnl, a firm best known for its highly customizable E Ink dashboards that can function as anything from a desktop calendar to a stock tracker, has introduced a new display that’s also well suited for showing artwork and photos. It’s not the company’s first color E Ink device, but instead of being limited to just four colors, the new Frame can display thousands of shades using a 31.5-inch E Ink Spectra 6 panel, similar to what you’ll find in products from Aura and Pocketbook.

    The Frame is now available for preorder for $1,299 in a handmade wooden body and you can choose from four different types of wood: white oak, cherry, sapele, and walnut. The first batch will be a limited run of around 470 units that’s already more than half sold out, and delivery of most of the displays is expected to happen in early 2027. Optional add-ons include a matching wooden kickstand if you don’t want to hang it on a wall, and a larger 20,000mAh battery. However, the Frame should run for months between charges with the standard 10,000mAh option.

    What sets the Frame apart from other large format E Ink art frames and posters is that it’s open source and can do more than display images. Through plugins you can build yourself, or download from a marketplace featuring over 1,400 at this point, the Frame can also be used as a dashboard showing the weather, to-do lists, or whatever info you want hanging on your wall.

    If you do use it for displaying imagery, Trmnl developed Lazarus, a color conversion engine the company believes provides the “best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display.” If you disagree, because the Frame is open source, you can adjust the color tuning to match your own preferences.

    Recent findings suggest that as with Trmnl’s other E Ink products, the Frame can be connected to the internet to dynamically display whatever information you need it to. But to further extend its battery life, you can also fill a microSD card with a folder of images files and use the Frame offline. You can customize how frequently a new photo is displayed, or set up schedules so that your favorite piece of art stays on screen longer than others. While the Frame is more expensive than other E Ink Spectra 6 products currently available, the appeal here is the flexibility to use it as more than just a digital poster.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Meta is testing Direct, a latest standalone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages.
    • With Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain owners who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging.
    • Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the firm says it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Meta is testing Direct, a latest standalone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages. Direct is initially launching in Turkey and Thailand, and can be used with or without an Instagram account.

    With Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain owners who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging. Over the years, people have often sought out various ways to use Instagram’s direct messaging features without having to deal with the rest of the platform.

    Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the firm says it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.

    The fresh app also gives the organization a way to keep these customers within its ecosystem rather than risk losing them altogether, and count them as active users within its ecosystem even if they don’t use Instagram itself.

    Besides usual messaging features like reactions, voice notes and emojis, Direct also features a “Draw” feature that lets you doodle and sketch directly inside chat threads. There’s also “Notes,” which are the short status updates that appear at the top of your Instagram DMs.

    Meta claims owners can create custom stickers, add audio effects to replies, and personalize chat backgrounds with custom themes.

    Meta notes only people in your contacts or those you’re already connected with can start conversations or add you to group chats. Users can also report, block, restrict, or remove contacts at any time.

    It has been revealed that the tech giant also claims it will use its age-estimation technology to identify and address potentially inappropriate interactions involving young people. Parents will also have access to supervision tools that let them see who their teens are messaging, manage safety settings, and set daily usage limits.

    Teens who use their Instagram username and password to access Direct will have to work with all the same messaging restrictions as Instagram’s Teen Accounts.

    Meta did not say when or if it will bring Direct to additional countries.

    The NDLEA remarked the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.

    Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

    A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

    #12267. Five EU states announce aims for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (797 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Five EU states announce aims for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’.
    • Five EU member states have unveiled plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
    • The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’.

    Five EU member states have unveiled plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

    The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

    In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

    Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

    In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

    Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

    The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

    The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

    Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, remarked it was “a huge breakthrough”.

    The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, noted: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”.

    According to recent reports, andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”.

    Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

    Recent findings suggest that spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, mentioned on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.

    Recent findings suggest that the French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She stated: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”.

    Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, remarked it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

    In a recent development, “On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he stated. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

    Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

    Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

    #12266. Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes off in Texas, with dozens of cities to follow

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (627 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes off in Texas, with dozens of cities to follow

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership revealed earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.
    • Industry observers note that the commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas.
    • Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership revealed earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.

    Industry observers note that the commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline proposal to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

    Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.

    Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a latest “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber mentioned that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal will offer drone delivery.

    “In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a latest expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton stated in a statement that underscores those aspirations.

    Sources indicate that those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those looks have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.

    Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have mentioned.

    And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the the communities where they services are available.

    It has been revealed that zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based organization’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled swiftly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.

    Sources indicate that uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither manufacturer has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global and that included backing by Uber, among others.
